warmup.q: The payments company keeps its payments in a Kafka log, and two programs read it: the ledger and the fraud check. The ledger has read every payment so far. The fraud check is 3,000 payments behind. What happens to the payments the ledger has already read?
options: Kafka deletes them as soon as the ledger says it has read them
They stay until the log's age or size limit removes them, whoever has read them
Kafka keeps them until the fraud check has read them too, then deletes them
Kafka moves them to a waiting list that only the fraud check can see
warmup.why: Reading never deletes anything in Kafka. Each reader keeps one number, the place of the next payment it will read, and the payments stay where they are. They leave only when the log's retention, a limit on age or size, removes old data (Partitions and segments on disk, the next lesson, shows how), and that limit ignores readers. The first and third options describe the broker queue of Queues and brokers, which deletes a message once it's acknowledged. That's the habit to unlearn here.

sections.h: Keep every payment, and give each reader a bookmark: the log
sections.html:
Let's start where Queues and brokers stopped. The payments program sent each payment through a broker, a program in the middle that holds messages, and the broker did its job. No payment was lost while the fraud check restarted, and the payments program stopped waiting for anyone. But the broker kept a state for every message (waiting, delivered, to whom), and deleted it once a consumer had acknowledged it, that is, said it was done.

That choice cost three things. To feed four programs, the broker kept four queues, with a copy of every payment in each. A fifth program that wants the payments starts with nothing, because last week's are gone. When a bug in the fee calculation means yesterday's payments must be worked through again, the queue can't give them back. And two copies of one program, sharing one queue, booked an account's payments out of order.

A log makes the opposite choice: keep every message, and let each reader track its own place. The payments program adds each payment to the end of a file that only grows. Every payment gets a number, its place in the file: 0, 1, 2 and so on. Each reader remembers one thing, the number of the next payment it wants. Reading changes nothing in the file. So four programs, or forty, read the same payments at their own pace from one copy. A new program can start at payment 0. And working through yesterday again means moving one number back.

That's the family chat from the start. The chat is the log, each post is a payment, and each phone's "you stopped here" is a reader's number. The picture breaks in two places. A chat may hide old posts from a new member, while a log shows them to anyone. And a chat lets you edit or delete a post, while a log never changes a record once it's written.

So a log is an ordered list of records that only grows at the end. Keep this picture for the whole track: one file you only add to, and a bookmark for each reader. Every later lesson of this track splits the log up, copies it to other machines or reads it in a cleverer way.

Kafka has its own names for the parts. A record is one message in the log. In Kafka it has a key (what it's about, such as an account), a value (the payment itself), a timestamp and optional headers, extra labelled fields. A broker, in Kafka, is the program that keeps logs on its disk and answers other programs over the network. A producer is a program that adds records, and a consumer is one that reads them. A topic is the name they use, such as payments. Kafka stores each topic as one or more partitions, and each partition is one log. This lesson's topics have a single partition, so here topic, partition and log mean the same thing. The next lesson splits a topic into many.

The log keeps everything, but it still has to say which record is which. Next, we'll see how Kafka numbers them.

video.title: The log: appends, offsets and one bookmark per reader

sections.h: Every record gets a number that never changes: its offset
sections.html:
Here is a log after the payments program added five records. You'll build exactly this one in the Try it below:

offset  key      value
0       acct-17  auth 40.00 EUR
1       acct-42  auth 12.50 EUR
2       acct-17  capture 40.00 EUR
3       acct-99  auth 300.00 EUR
4       acct-42  refund 12.50 EUR

The number on the left is the record's offset: its place in the log, counting from 0. The key says which account the record is about, and the value says what happened. auth is the authorization, when the bank sets the money aside. capture is when the money really moves to the shop, and refund gives it back.

The broker gives each record its offset when the record arrives. The producer never picks it; it learns the number from the broker's reply:

Java
var record = new ProducerRecord<>("payments", "acct-17", "auth 40.00 EUR");
RecordMetadata md = producer.send(record).get();   // waits for the broker's reply
System.out.println(md.offset());                   // the broker chose this number
Kotlin
val record = ProducerRecord("payments", "acct-17", "auth 40.00 EUR")
val md = producer.send(record).get()               // waits for the broker's reply
println(md.offset())                               // the broker chose this number

A ProducerRecord is one record to send: the topic, the key and the value. send returns at once with a future, an object that will hold the answer once it arrives, and get() waits for it. The answer, RecordMetadata, says where the record landed. The Kotlin version makes the same calls, with val and without new.

Three rules make offsets useful. First, an offset never changes: record 2 is the capture for account 17 today, next week and every time anyone reads the log again. Second, Kafka never reuses an offset within a partition. Even after old records are deleted (the next lesson shows how), the next record gets the next number. If offsets 0 to 799 existed and the oldest 300 were deleted, the next record still gets 800. Third, nothing is inserted or edited. You can't put a record between 1 and 2, and you can't change record 3. To correct something, you add a new record. That's why the capture and the refund above are records of their own: the log is the history of what happened, in the order it happened.

Together, these rules make an offset a permanent name for one record. When a consumer says "I've dealt with everything before offset 4", or a bug report says "look at offset 3", everyone means the same record.

One more number. The end offset is the offset the next record will get: 5 in the log above. Kafka's tools call it the log end offset, or LEO. Every offset below it exists; nothing at or above it has been written yet.

You've met this structure before. A database such as PostgreSQL writes every change to a log on disk, its write-ahead log, before it touches a table (Write-ahead logging and crash recovery, in the Storage engines track). Jay Kreps, one of Kafka's creators, built his 2013 essay "The Log" on that idea. If several programs read the same ordered log and apply each record the same way, they all end up in the same state. Kafka turns such a log into something many programs share.

So far there's a log and its numbers. Next, we'll see what a reader has to remember, and why it's so little.

try.title: Append five payments and read them back
steps: From the labs folder, start one Kafka broker: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait. Docker is a tool that runs programs in sealed boxes called containers, and this command starts Kafka 4.4 in one, in the background. It's ready in about 5 seconds.

Open a shell, a command prompt, inside it with docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka bash, and run the commands below. Kafka comes with small command-line tools. These create a topic with one partition, add five payments with keys using the console producer, and read them back with their offsets using the console consumer.
Predict, then run the consumer command a second time. Which offsets come back?
Keep the broker and the shell open. The next Try its use them.

code.title: inside the kafka container
code.html: cd /opt/kafka/bin ./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic payments --partitions 1 printf 'acct-17:auth 40.00 EUR\nacct-42:auth 12.50 EUR\nacct-17:capture 40.00 EUR\nacct-99:auth 300.00 EUR\nacct-42:refund 12.50 EUR\n' \ | ./kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic payments \ --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=: ./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic payments --from-beginning \ --max-messages 5 --formatter-property print.offset=true --formatter-property print.key=true

try.expect:
Created topic payments.
The consumer rebalance protocol (KIP-848) is production-ready! Set group.protocol=consumer to try it out. ...
Offset:0	acct-17	auth 40.00 EUR
Offset:1	acct-42	auth 12.50 EUR
Offset:2	acct-17	capture 40.00 EUR
Offset:3	acct-99	auth 300.00 EUR
Offset:4	acct-42	refund 12.50 EUR
Processed a total of 5 messages

The second run prints the same five lines: the first read removed nothing. The KIP-848 line is a notice the Kafka 4.4 tools print about a newer way for consumers to share work (Consumer groups and rebalancing, lesson 8 of this track); you can ignore it here. The older --property flag still works in 4.4 but is on its way out; --reader-property and --formatter-property are the new names.

sections.h: What a reader remembers is one number: its position
sections.html:
Every reader has to remember where it is. After a restart, it should neither skip records nor handle them twice. What's the least it can store?

The broker queue of Queues and brokers stored a state for every message: delivered to whom, acknowledged or not, returned how often. With a million messages and four consumer programs, that's four million entries for the broker to keep. A log needs far less. Its records are in a fixed order and never change, so a reader that has handled everything before offset 50 can describe its whole state with one number: 50. That number is the reader's position, the offset of the next record it will read. Kafka's design documentation says it directly: for each partition, a consumer's position is a single whole number. Reading means asking the broker for records starting at the position, then moving the position past what came back.

A position kept only in memory is lost when the program restarts. So consumers that work together form a consumer group: a named set of consumers that read a topic as one, such as the group ledger. The group saves its position in Kafka itself, in a topic Kafka keeps for the purpose, __consumer_offsets. Saving it is a commit, and the saved number is the committed offset. The reference documentation of Kafka's Java consumer, KafkaConsumer, is clear that it should be the offset of the next record your program will read, not the last one it finished. Get that wrong by one, and every restart skips a record or repeats one. Lesson 7 of this track, Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees, covers commits in depth.

You don't need a group just to read. A consumer can take a partition directly with assign and set its position with seek:

Java
TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition("payments", 0);   // topic payments, partition 0
consumer.assign(List.of(tp));     // no group: this consumer just takes partition 0
consumer.seek(tp, 50);            // the next poll starts at offset 50
ConsumerRecords<String, String> batch = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
Kotlin
val tp = TopicPartition("payments", 0)                    // topic payments, partition 0
consumer.assign(listOf(tp))       // no group: this consumer just takes partition 0
consumer.seek(tp, 50)             // the next poll starts at offset 50
val batch = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))

A TopicPartition names one partition, here partition 0 of payments. assign takes it, with no group. seek sets the position to 50, and poll fetches records from there. The Kotlin version only drops new, the types and the semicolons.

Because a position is only a number, going back is cheap. You fixed a bug in the fee calculation and need to work out yesterday's payouts again? Seek back and read again. A new reporting program needs history? It starts at the oldest offset Kafka still has. Neither one changes anything for any other reader. The stepper below shows two groups and one job with no group, each with its own number.

One thing about poll: it returns whatever the broker had ready within the time you gave it, up to max.poll.records (500 by default). That can be fewer records than you wanted, or none at all, especially on the first call, while the consumer is still connecting. Code that needs "the next 10 records" has to loop until it has them or a deadline passes. You'll write that loop in the lab.

One number per reader, and records that never move. Next, we'll see what that means when many readers share one log.

code.title: ReadFromOffsetDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.msg.l02.demo; import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.Admin; import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.NewTopic; import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.ConsumerRecord; import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.KafkaConsumer; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.RecordMetadata; import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition; import org.apache.kafka.common.errors.TopicExistsException; import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer; import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer; import java.time.Duration; import java.time.LocalTime; import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** Appends 100 payments to a one-partition topic, then reads 5 of them back starting at offset 50. */ public class ReadFromOffsetDemo { static final String TOPIC = "payment-events"; static final String BOOTSTRAP = "localhost:9092"; // env/kafka.yml public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // 1. make sure the topic exists: one partition, so one log try (Admin admin = Admin.create(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP))) { admin.createTopics(List.of(new NewTopic(TOPIC, 1, (short) 1))).all().get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { if (!(e.getCause() instanceof TopicExistsException)) throw e; } // 2. append 100 records; the broker answers each one with the offset it got String sentAt = LocalTime.now().truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.SECONDS).toString(); try (var producer = new KafkaProducer<String, String>(Map.of( "bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "key.serializer", StringSerializer.class, "value.serializer", StringSerializer.class))) { List<Future<RecordMetadata>> acks = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) { acks.add(producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>(TOPIC, "acct-" + (i % 7), "payment-" + i + " sent at " + sentAt))); } long first = acks.get(0).get().offset(); long last = acks.get(99).get().offset(); System.out.printf("appended 100 records at offsets %d..%d%n", first, last); } // 3. read 5 records starting at offset 50: no group, just assign and seek TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition(TOPIC, 0); try (var consumer = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(Map.of( "bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class))) { consumer.assign(List.of(tp)); consumer.seek(tp, 50); System.out.println("reading from offset 50:"); List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> got = new ArrayList<>(); while (got.size() < 5) { for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))) { if (got.size() < 5) got.add(r); } } for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : got) { System.out.printf(" offset %d key %s value %s%n", r.offset(), r.key(), r.value()); } System.out.printf("end offset of the partition: %d%n", consumer.endOffsets(List.of(tp)).get(tp)); } } }

sections.h: Reading deletes nothing, so every reader gets every record
sections.html:
If no read removes anything, what does? Only retention: a limit, set for each topic, on how old or how large the data may get. By default, Kafka keeps a topic's data for 7 days (retention.ms is 604,800,000 milliseconds) and then deletes the old part, a whole file at a time. Who has read what plays no part. The next lesson shows the files and the rules.

Any number of consumer groups can read the same partition, and each group gets every record. The ledger and the fraud check are two groups. Each has its own committed offset, and neither can move the other's. In the chat, that's every phone keeping its own "you stopped here".

Four things follow from this, and each one comes back later in this track.

A slow consumer doesn't slow down the producer or the other groups. It only falls behind. That's the log's answer to a question from Queues and brokers, what to do when producers outrun consumers: it keeps the records on disk, up to retention, instead of pushing back on producers. The distance between the end offset and a group's committed offset is its lag. If the end offset is 1,250 and the fraud check has committed 40, its lag is 1,210 records.

A consumer that crashes starts again from its last committed offset. Whatever it handled after that commit, it handles again. So Kafka's default promise is at-least-once delivery: every record is handled at least once, and some may be handled twice. That's why a payments consumer needs an idempotency key, an id on every payment, and skips ids it has already booked.

Replay is cheap and safe. A new group can read a topic from the oldest offset still kept, and an existing group can move its committed offset back.

Order exists only inside one partition. Two partitions are two separate logs, and nothing orders a record in one against a record in the other. The next lesson deals with that.

There's a flip side to keeping everything. A record stays for the whole retention period, on every copy of the log, readable by any program allowed to read the topic, however many times it has been read. So never write anything to a topic that you aren't allowed to keep for days, such as full card numbers.

Reading moves a bookmark; only retention deletes. Choose each topic's retention on purpose.

One more name, so it doesn't surprise you later. Kafka 4.2 made share groups ready for real use. They hand each record to one member of a group and acknowledge records one by one, like the queue of Queues and brokers, on top of a topic. Lesson 11 of this track covers them. Every lesson before that uses ordinary consumer groups, which work as described here.

That's what the log promises. Next, we'll see how one broker keeps that promise at tens of thousands of records a second.

sections.h: Why adding to the end is fast: the disk and the page cache
sections.html:
A busy broker might take 50,000 records a second. Can a disk keep up with that?

It depends on where the writes go. A spinning disk has to move its head to the right place before each write. That move, a seek, takes about 5 to 10 ms, so writes to random places top out at a few hundred a second. Writing at the end of one file needs almost no seeking: the head stays where it is, and the data streams on. Reading or writing straight through like that is called sequential I/O (input and output). Kafka's design documentation gives the numbers from its test disks: about 600 MB/s for sequential writes, against about 100 kB/s for random ones. An SSD, a disk made of memory chips with no moving parts, narrows the gap a lot: a random 4 KB read on a fast one (an NVMe SSD) takes about 0.1 ms. But sequential I/O still wins, and it lets the operating system do most of the work.

That work happens in the page cache. The kernel, the core of the operating system, keeps copies of recently read and written file data in spare memory. When the broker adds to a log file, the kernel puts the bytes in the page cache and writes them to disk a little later. When a consumer reads near the end of the log, which describes almost every healthy consumer, the data was written seconds ago and is still in memory. Copying 4 KB from memory takes well under a microsecond, against about 100 microseconds from an SSD.

Kafka runs on the JVM, the program that runs Java code, and it keeps no cache of records in the JVM's own memory, its heap. It relies on the page cache instead. That's why brokers usually run with a heap of a few gigabytes on machines with far more memory: the rest is page cache. (The page cache, writeback and fsync, in the Operating systems track, opened it up.)

Two more choices keep the cost down. Records travel in batches: the producer groups records for the same partition, and in the common case the broker stores each batch as it arrived and hands it to consumers the same way. And when it can, the broker uses sendfile, a system call (a request a program makes to the kernel), to send file data from the page cache straight to the network, without copying it through the JVM. That shortcut, called zero-copy, isn't used when connections are encrypted (with TLS), because the broker must scramble the data itself first.

Finding a record is cheap too. Adding a record costs the same however long the log is, because it always goes at the end. A read at an offset finds the right file, looks up a small index and reads forward. The next lesson opens those files.

The weak spot is a consumer that falls far behind. It reads old data that's no longer in the page cache, so those reads go to the disk, and they can push recent data out of memory. One slow batch job, a program that reads a big pile of old records in one go, can slow down every reader near the end on the same broker.

A log that only grows is fast to add to, and it will fill any disk in the end. The next lesson deals with that.

opening:
Picture a family group chat. Your aunt posts a photo, and everyone reads it in their own time. Each phone remembers where its owner stopped reading. Your reading deletes nothing for anyone else, and you can scroll back to last week.

Now the payments company wants a new program to study last week's payments. With the broker from the last lesson, it gets nothing: each payment was deleted once the other programs had read it.

It's easy to think a message is used up once it's read. Letters, to-do lists and broker queues all work that way. A chat doesn't.

Queues and brokers left three problems open: no past for a new reader, no second reading, and lost order. In this lesson, we'll build the chat's model, a log, the idea at the heart of Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages on disk and lets many programs read them. We'll number every record, give each reader one number, and see why adding to the end is fast. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a family chat where reading deletes nothing and every phone keeps its own place. A Kafka partition works the same way: records stay at fixed offsets, and each reader is one number. That's why a new program can read last week's payments without anyone else noticing.

Leave a busy group chat unread for a day, then open it. Does the app take you to where you stopped, or to the newest message? Either way, it saved one number for you, the way a consumer group commits its offset.

Next, we'll split one log into many and cut each one into files, and ask how a log that only grows can still forget.

compare.title: Read ten records from offset 50 in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: static List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> readTen(KafkaConsumer<String, String> consumer) { TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition("payments", 0); consumer.assign(List.of(tp)); consumer.seek(tp, 50); List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> out = new ArrayList<>(); long deadline = System.nanoTime() + Duration.ofSeconds(5).toNanos(); while (out.size() < 10 && System.nanoTime() < deadline) { for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200)).records(tp)) { if (out.size() < 10) out.add(r); } } return out; }

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: fun readTen(consumer: KafkaConsumer<String, String>): List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> { val tp = TopicPartition("payments", 0) consumer.assign(listOf(tp)) consumer.seek(tp, 50) val out = mutableListOf<ConsumerRecord<String, String>>() val deadline = System.nanoTime() + Duration.ofSeconds(5).toNanos() while (out.size < 10 && System.nanoTime() < deadline) { out += consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200)).records(tp).take(10 - out.size) } return out }

compare.note: Both call the same Java library. Kotlin uses listOf where Java uses List.of, adds a whole list with +=, and uses take to stop at ten. records(tp) returns a Java List, so Kotlin's collection functions work on it directly. Neither version commits anything: with assign and no group.id, there's no group to commit to.

worked.title: Read one partition again from offset 50, up to where it ended when you started

steps.say: An audit job must read partition 0 of payments again from offset 50 and stop at the end. But the end moves: producers keep adding records while you read. So pin it first, by asking for the end offset before reading anything.
steps.code: // 1. pin the end: the offset the next record would get, right now TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition("payments", 0); consumer.assign(List.of(tp)); long stopAt = consumer.endOffsets(List.of(tp)).get(tp);

alt.html: // 1. pin the end: the offset the next record would get, right now val tp = TopicPartition("payments", 0) consumer.assign(listOf(tp)) val stopAt = consumer.endOffsets(listOf(tp)).getValue(tp)

steps.say: Set the position. seek only changes a number inside the client; the next poll fetches from there.
steps.code: // 2. set the position consumer.seek(tp, 50);

alt.html: // 2. set the position consumer.seek(tp, 50)

steps.say: Read until the position reaches the pinned end. consumer.position(tp) is the offset of the next record the consumer will return, which makes it the natural place to stop. Records at stopAt or later arrived after you started; leave them for the next run. reconcile(r) stands for the job's own check of one record.
steps.code: // 3. read until the position reaches the pinned end while (consumer.position(tp) < stopAt) { for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)).records(tp)) { if (r.offset() >= stopAt) break; // arrived after we started reconcile(r); } }

alt.html: // 3. read until the position reaches the pinned end while (consumer.position(tp) < stopAt) { for (r in consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)).records(tp)) { if (r.offset() >= stopAt) break // arrived after we started reconcile(r) } }

steps.say: Notice what's missing: no group.id and no commit. If the job crashes, you run it again from 50. For a one-off replay, that's the simplest correct design. A job that must pick up where it stopped needs a group and commits, which lesson 7 of this track covers.

lab.title: Build a log in memory, then read a real one
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 12 fail: the stubs (methods left for you to write) throw NotImplementedError or UnsupportedOperationException. The first run also downloads the apache/kafka-native:4.4.0 image (about 150 MB), a packaged Kafka broker that the tests start in a container; after that, the broker starts in a second or two.
In MiniLog.kt, write endOffset, append and read. Offsets have no gaps and start at 0, so the next offset is the number of records so far. read returns a copy, and rejects a from outside 0..endOffset.
Write LogReader.poll and LogReader.seek. A reader's whole state is position: read from it, then move it forward by the number of records you got.
Run the tests. The eight tests in MiniLogTest should pass now.
In OffsetReader.java, write readFrom: assign, seek, then a poll loop with a deadline that keeps at most max records.
Run the tests until all 12 pass. OffsetReaderTest runs your code against a real Kafka 4.4 broker in a container.
hints: records.subList(a, b) is a view of the list, not a copy. Wrap it with .toList(), so a caller never sees later appends through it.

In readFrom, consumer.poll(...).records(tp) gives you only that partition's records. The loop needs two ways out: enough records, or the deadline has passed. Without the deadline, a read at the end of the partition never returns.
If only the broker tests fail with a Docker error, check that Docker Desktop is running. MiniLogTest needs no Docker.

drill.title: Write the replay loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. Write replay(consumer, topic, partition, from): it reads one partition from offset from up to the end offset as it was when the function started, and returns the values in order. No group, no commits. Then compare with the answer. Did you pin the end offset before the loop?

answer.html: static List<String> replay(Consumer<String, String> consumer, String topic, int partition, long from) { TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition(topic, partition); consumer.assign(List.of(tp)); long stopAt = consumer.endOffsets(List.of(tp)).get(tp); // pin the end first consumer.seek(tp, from); List<String> values = new ArrayList<>(); while (consumer.position(tp) < stopAt) { for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)).records(tp)) { if (r.offset() < stopAt) values.add(r.value()); } } return values; }

alt.html: fun replay(consumer: Consumer<String, String>, topic: String, partition: Int, from: Long): List<String> { val tp = TopicPartition(topic, partition) consumer.assign(listOf(tp)) val stopAt = consumer.endOffsets(listOf(tp)).getValue(tp) // pin the end first consumer.seek(tp, from) val values = mutableListOf<String>() while (consumer.position(tp) < stopAt) { consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)).records(tp) .filter { it.offset() < stopAt } .mapTo(values) { it.value() } } return values }

recap: A broker's queue deletes a message once it's acked; a log keeps every record. A Kafka partition is a log: an ordered list of records that only grows at the end, and the broker gives each record the next offset, starting at 0.
An offset never changes and is never reused within a partition, so it names one record for good. The end offset is the number the next record will get.
A reader's whole state is one number per partition, its position: the offset of the next record. A consumer group saves it in __consumer_offsets as its committed offset.
Reading never deletes. Retention removes old data by age or size, whoever has read it, so every group gets every record, and a slow group only builds up lag.
assign plus seek reads from any offset without a group, so replay costs nothing. Adding at the end and reading near it are fast, because both are sequential and mostly served from the page cache.
The limit: inside a group, one log has one reader at a time, and a log that only grows will fill any disk. The next lesson splits a topic into partitions and cuts each one into files.

explain.prompt: A friend who has used broker queues for years asks: "When my consumer acknowledges a Kafka message, where does the message go?" Explain what really happens, and what decides when the record is deleted.
explain.answer: It goes nowhere. Acknowledging in Kafka means committing an offset: the consumer group saves one number per partition, the offset of the next record it will read. The record stays in the partition's log at the same offset, and every other group can still read it, now or later. Kafka deletes old records only through retention, by age (7 days by default) or by size, a whole file at a time. So a commit only changes where your group starts again after a restart, and reading a day again is only a matter of moving that number back.

deeper.html:
Jay Kreps' 2013 essay "The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction" is worth an evening. (It was published on the LinkedIn engineering blog. The original page has moved, so search for the title.) Its core argument: a log is the simplest structure that puts all events in one order, and any program that always does the same thing for the same input, reading the same log from the same start, ends up in the same state. Databases already work this way inside. Replication, keeping copies of a database on other machines, is mostly shipping the log to them.

Two ideas from that line of thinking come back later in the course. A table is a log folded down to the latest value for each key. Kafka Streams calls this the stream-table duality (Kafka Streams: tables, state and windows, in the Stream processing track), and log compaction (the next lesson) keeps exactly that latest value per key on disk. And change data capture turns a database's own log into Kafka records (Two systems, one truth: dual writes and change data capture, in the same track). Debezium, a free tool that does this, reads PostgreSQL's write-ahead log, or the change log of another database, and publishes each change in the order it was committed.

One detail to keep straight: an offset is a number in a sequence, not a position in a file. Records vary in size, so the broker can't work out where offset 50 starts in the file. Each log file has a small index from offsets to byte positions, with an entry every few kilobytes, and the next lesson opens it.
